title: Kachoris and Coffee: Why Food Has Become the New Fuel for India's Run Clubs
excerpt: Across Indian cities, post-run kachoris, modak and tiramisu have turned sunrise runs into the new social outing for a sober-curious generation.
body:
• Food has become the new fuel for India's run clubs — for many members, the promise of post-run kachoris, modak or tiramisu is as big a draw as the run itself, according to India Today.
  • New collectives like the Delhi Run Collective grew from 10 runners to nearly 100 Sunday participants in two years, with "post-run meals and banter" as the social glue, per Indulge Express.
  • Morning groups routinely end sessions with breakfast or coffee, turning workouts into a "third place" outside home and work, per The Impressive Times.
  • The shift is a sober-curious Gen Z trade: bars and pub crawls out, sunrise runs and daytime wellness events in, with cafés doubling as community spaces, per iDiva.

Opening news lead

At 5 am in Indian cities, runners are no longer lacing up for the pace chart. They are running for the food. India Today reported on September 21, 2026 that kachoris, tiramisu and modak have become the new fuel for run clubs — the reward at the end of the route and, increasingly, the reason some members show up at all.

Context & Background

The run-club boom is only a few years old. In Delhi, the Delhi Run Collective — launched two years ago by Shahnil Samantara, Manraj Singh and Krishna Lohiya — grew from 10 people at its first Instagram-posted run to nearly 100 runners on Sundays, mostly working professionals between 25 and 30, according to Indulge Express. Before these collectives, Delhi's running community belonged to marathoners in their 40s and 50s. "Younger people didn't really have an outlet," Samantara told Indulge Express. The new clubs play by different rules, prioritising community over race timings.

"When we run in a group, it's about company, fun, pushing each other, post-run meals and banter — it becomes a hangout."

— Mohit Solanki, runner

The food lowers the pressure. For those who do not care about racing, the shared meal supplies the belonging. Roktim Chakraborty, 29, told Indulge Express that running has restructured his weekends: "boring Sundays" became long-run Sundays, with "a different kind of satisfaction in starting your day early and finishing a long run before most people are even awake."

Impact & Analysis

The pattern repeats across the country. In Bhubaneswar, a Gen Z-focused running club has combined early-morning exercise with friendship, mental wellbeing and community, drawing students and young professionals, according to The Impressive Times. iDiva reports that cafés are doubling as community spaces and that "morning runs that end with coffee" are attracting people looking for more than exercise.

This is the "third place" in action: the social environment outside home and workplace where relationships form. Food is its anchor because it is the most democratic part of the ritual — you do not need to be fast to eat together. As marathoner Surjanu Chaudhari, 42, put it to Indulge Express: "Running becomes a natural ice-breaker." The shared table extends that past the finish line.

"People arrive for the activity but often return for the community."

— iDiva

The women-only clubs show how intentional the space has become: Juby George founded Trail Femmes in 2024 after years of being one of few women in running groups, and Delhi Run Collective added a women-only vertical in December 2025, managed by Soumya Singh. Runners say these spaces allow conversations — about career breaks, injuries, beginner anxieties — that rarely happen in mixed groups. The post-run food table is part of that safe space.

Diaspora Angle

For Indians abroad, the trend lands on familiar ground: diaspora run clubs from the Bay Area to Dubai already end long runs at a dosa joint or chai cart. NRIs visiting India can treat a local run club as a low-barrier social entry — show up before sunrise, run at your own pace, eat with strangers, leave with friends.

What's Next

The race calendar keeps feeding the clubs — the Vedanta Delhi Half Marathon is set for October 18, with the Pinkathon following in March, per Indulge Express — and each big race funnels new runners into the morning groups. The ones that last will be those that protect what made them work: low pressure, early mornings, a shared table at the end. As The Impressive Times put it, the question is increasingly not "how many calories did I burn?" but "will I come back next week?" In India, the answer increasingly depends on what is waiting at breakfast.
image_caption: An India Today illustration shows runners alongside modaks, kachoris and tiramisu. India's run clubs are pulling in members with post-run food spreads, from dawn kachori runs to tiramisu meetups.
nri_angle: Diaspora run clubs already end long runs at dosa joints and chai carts, and NRIs visiting India can use local run clubs as a low-barrier way to build a social circle.
author: Diaspora Desk
